title: TC0-00649
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review (from the opening paragraphs): He asks the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) to allow his appeal and substitute a positive decision or return his claim to the RPD for redetermination.
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: XXXX XXXX XXXX (the Appellant) is citizen of Jamaica. His claim for refugee protection, based on his fear of gang members was rejected by the Refugee Protection Division (RPD). The Appellant argues that the RPD made errors of fact and law. He asks the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) to allow his appeal and substitute a positive decision or return his claim to the RPD for redetermination.
I dismiss the appeal. The RPD was correct in finding that the Appellant is neither a Convention refugee, nor a person in need of protection.

The Appellant alleged before the RPD that his neighbourhood was subject to ongoing gang violence. His brother was killed in XXXX 2018 when he was caught in crossfire between the police and gang members while leaving the Appellant's house. Shortly after he brother's death, the Appellant was threatened by a gang. He alleges a risk of harm from one of the neighbourhood gangs due to his childhood friendship with a rival gang leader. The Appellant was alleged to be an informer. The Appellant left Jamaica on XXXX XXXX, 2018 and arrived in Canada. Since he left Jamaica, the Appellant's wife has received threats from the gang.

The Appellant's claim for refugee protection was heard by the RPD on November 15, 2019. In a written decision dated December 17, 2019, the RPD rejected his claim, finding he had not established a nexus to a Convention refugee ground, and that he had not credibly established that he would be at risk of targeted violence if he were to return to Jamaica. The RPD found that the Appellant's childhood friendship with a gang leader was insufficient to establish that the risk of harm was personalized, in the absence of any other evidence.

On appeal, it is argued that the RPD unreasonably imposed a higher standard of proof on the Appellant than required and did not consider that he faces more than a mere possibility of persecution should he return to Jamaica. He further submits that the RPD erred by giving no weight to documentary evidence and by concluding his risk was generalized. He submits that the RPD decision was replete with errors of law and fact.

The determinative issue on appeal is whether the Appellant has credibly established a personalized risk to his life in Jamaica. I find that he did not demonstrate on a balance of probabilities that he is subject to a personalized risk in Jamaica. I agree with the RPD that the Appellant has not established that he was directly targeted by gang members. The RPD was correct in finding that his fear of return to Jamaica relates to the situation of generalized criminality in that country. Request for an Oral Hearing

The Appellant has requested an oral hearing.1 The RAD may hold a hearing if, in its opinion, there is documentary evidence referred to in subsection 110(3) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA) that raises a serious issue with respect to the credibility of the person who is the subject of the appeal, is central to the decision with respect to the refugee protection claim, and, if accepted, would justify allowing or rejecting the refugee protection claim.2
Given that the Appellant has not submitted any new evidence, I am unable to hold a hearing.
My role is to look at all the evidence and decide if the RPD made the correct decision.3 Standard of Proof

The RPD found that the Appellant's situation did not fall under the umbrella of section 96 of the IRPA. The RPD did not find any evidence of a nexus between the Appellant's circumstances and a Convention ground and therefore only assessed the claim under section 97 of the IRPA. The RPD found that the Appellant had not established, on a balance of probabilities, that he was being pursued by gang members or that he would be at risk of targeted violence if he was to return to Jamaica. The RPD found, after considering the totality of the evidence, that the Appellant is not a Convention refugee pursuant to section 96 of the IRPA or a person in need of protection under subsection 97(1) of the IRPA.

The Appellant argues that the RPD imposed a higher standard of proof by requiring proof that he would be persecuted, as opposed to the proper test, which only requires a reasonable chance or more than a mere possibility of persecution.

I have reviewed the record and have considered the Appellant's allegations. I agree with the RPD that the Appellant has not established a nexus to a Convention ground. I find that what he fears in Jamaica is criminality. Case law has established that victims of crime, corruption or vendettas cannot usually establish a link between their fear of persecution and one of the five grounds in the definition of a Convention refugee. 4 I find that the RPD did not err by assessing the claim under section 97 of the IRPA, given the Appellant's personal circumstances. An individual claiming to be a person in need of protection within the ambit of paragraph 97(1)(b) must prove, on a balance of probabilities, that his return would personally subject him to a risk to life or to a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment in every part of that country of nationality that is not faced generally by other individuals in or from that country. There must be evidence of a specific personal risk faced prospectively by the claimant as opposed to an indiscriminate or random risk faced by the claimant and others.

I disagree with the Appellant that the RPD was required to assess whether that there was more than a mere possibility of persecution should he return to Jamaica, given that when assessing a claim under section 97 of the IRPA, a claimant must establish, on a balance of probabilities, that his return would personally subject him to a risk to life or to a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment. I find that there is no merit to the Appellant's argument that the RPD imposed a higher standard of proof than required by law. Generalized Risk

The RPD found that the Appellant had not established that there was a personalized risk of harm should he return to Jamaica. The RPD considered his testimony that he began receiving indirect threats after his brother was killed in XXXX 2018, from XXXX XXXX, the leader of one of the neighbourhood gangs. The Appellant was alleged to be an informer because he was childhood friends with another gang leader, XXXX XXXX. The RPD considered that family members of the Appellant who lived at the same address did not experience any problems and that the Appellant was not aware of any other neighbours or childhood friends of the gang leader XXXX XXXX experiencing problems. The RPD noted that the Appellant testified that he had no contact with XXXX.

The RPD reviewed the documentary evidence provided by the Appellant to support his claim. This included letters from his wife, two sisters and mother, as well as a document from the Jamaican police from XXXX 2009 indicating a report of a threat. The RAD found that these documents did not support the Appellant's allegation that he was being personally targeted by anyone. The RPD found that the letters from the family corroborated a generalized threat of gang violence but did not provide any particulars of threats to the Appellant himself or anything to establish a particularized risk to the Appellant.

The RPD considered the country conditions documentary evidence regarding high levels of violence faced daily by Jamaicans. The RPD concluded that the Appellant appeared to be resident in a dangerous neighbourhood and faces a generalized risk that many Jamaicans face.

The Appellant argues that the RPD failed to consider that police had to impose a curfew because of the high crime rate in the Appellant's area of Jamaica, and failed to accept that gangs have no respect for the police and will shoot them if they venture in their path. He submits that his life would be in great danger if he returned to Jamaica as there are killings every day in the country.

The Appellant submits that the RPD erred by not accepting that his life was threatened by XXXX XXXX because he was a childhood friend of a leader of a rival gang. He argues that the RPD also erred when it indicated that his family members were not experiencing any problems, even though the letters from these individuals indicate how dangerous it was to live in that area. He submits that the RPD made an error when stating that he resided in the same house with his uncle, nephews and sister, when they actually lived in different homes in the same neighbourhood.

The Appellant's claim for protection under subsection 97(1) of the IRPA requires an individualized assessment based on a two-step analysis of the claim. First, there must be an analysis of the personal risk in Jamaica, on a prospective basis. If a personal risk exists, then the second step is to determine whether the identified personal risk is one faced generally by the population.5 To be clear, the Appellant may face a personal risk if he returns to his country, but if the risk is found to be faced generally by others in or from that country, the Appellant will not be a person in need of protection pursuant to subsection 97(1) of the IRPA.

I have conducted an independent assessment of the record and agree with the RPD that the Appellant has not established that he faces a personalized risk of harm in Jamaica. I find that the claimant has not credibly established that he was being personally targeted by a gang leader named XXXX XXXX or any other gang members, group or individuals. While I concur with the Appellant that he resided in a very violent neighbourhood in Kingston, Jamaica, I find that his risk of harm should he return is a generalized one.

I have reviewed the information contained in the record relating to the harm feared by the Appellant. I note that he wrote in his Basis of Claim (BOC), in response to question 2(a), that he was sure the people who killed his brother would kill him. He stated in response to question 2(f) that he left Jamaica when he did because it became hard to live in the lane after his brother was killed as people began making threats against his family and saying that they would kill them and burn down his house where he lived with his wife and children. In the narrative portion of his BOC, he wrote that his brother was killed when caught in a crossfire between the police and gang members in the lane where the Appellant lived. He reiterated that his family was threatened with death and that their house would be burnt down.

The Appellant was questioned at the RPD hearing about what he feared in Jamaica, and he responded that after his brother was killed in 2018, he feared being killed by gang members who said he was an informer. He specifically noted that he feared a person named XXXX XXXX who was a gang leader. He additionally stated that he feared gang members in general. When asked for more details, the Appellant only provided information that the threats began after his brother was killed and that his wife was told about these threats by people in the neighbourhood. When asked why he was believed to be an informer, the Appellant stated that he had never informed, had not spoken to the police, and believed it was because he had been a childhood friend of the leader of another gang, who he was no longer in contact with. The RPD question the Appellant about what threat he would pose to XXXX and he replied that if you inform, you are a dead man.

The Appellant alleged at the hearing that his wife was threatened on the road in XXXX 2019 when going to pick up her daughter. When asked whether the threat was ongoing, he replied that people told her that they will kill her husband.

I have reviewed the supporting documents submitted by the Appellant. He has provided a Customer Reference Form issued by the Jamaican Constabulary Force dated XXXX XXXX XXXX 2019.6 In response to the heading Nature of Report it is noted "threat". The only name included in the report is that of the officer recording the crime. The report does not include the Appellant's wife's name, the name of the person making the threat or any details about what happened. I find that little weight can be put on this document to support the Appellant's allegations that threats were made to his wife in XXXX 2019.

I have reviewed the letter from the Appellant's wife dated XXXX XXXX, 2019.7 She writes in the letter that she is seeking asylum in Canada and wants to join her husband because she is currently living in fear for her life because of the violence in the area where she lives. She notes that she was recently threatened with violence by a gang and reported the incident to the police. She provides no details of the nature of the threat. I note that she makes no reference in the letter to threats made against her husband, the Appellant. I assign little weight to this letter in establishing that the Appellant was threatened by a gang leader named XXXX because he was believed to be an informer. I additionally note that there is no subsequent disclosure relating to ongoing threats against the Appellant or his family since that time.

The Appellant has provided a letter from his mother8 who notes that he had to flee Jamaica because there had been a lot of gang violence which continues to happen often and without warning. This letter to does not provide any details regarding the Appellant's specific fear of being targeted by XXXX or other gang members. I assign little weight to this letter in establishing the Appellant's allegations beyond the generalized violence that occurs in Jamaica.

The Appellant provided a letter from his sister XXXX, dated XXXX XXXX, 2018.9 It is stated in the letter that the Appellant had to flee Jamaica due to gang violence. There is a second letter from XXXX, dated XXXX XXXX XXXX 201910, in which she states she is seeking asylum in Canada for herself and her two children because she is currently living in fear due to increased violence in the area where she lives. There is no information in the letters regarding the Appellant being targeted by XXXX or other gang members and I assign them little weight in support of the allegations of the Appellant being personally targeted.

The Appellant has provided a letter from his sister XXXX, dated XXXX XXXX, 2018.11 This letter notes that he fled Jamaica for his safety, but makes no mention of the Appellant being targeted by XXXX or other gang members. As with the other letters, I assign it little weight in establishing the Appellant's allegations of targeted violence.

I find that the supporting letters provided by the Appellant can only establish that the Appellant left Jamaica because of the ongoing violence in the country, and in particular his neighbourhood, but are not probative in corroborating his allegations that he was targeted because he was believed to be an informer. I find it suspect that none of the documents provided by the Appellant to corroborate his claim make any mention of his allegations put forward at the hearing that he was being specifically targeted by a man named XXXX XXXX who believed that the Appellant was an informer. I find that it is reasonable to expect that if this had happened, information regarding being specifically targeted since his brother's death in XXXX 2018 would be corroborated by the Appellant's family members who were there at the time. Although the Appellant has argued that he did not live with his sister, uncle and nephews while in Jamaica, and the RPD erred by finding that he did, I note that he testified twice at the hearing that he did reside with these individuals in addition to his wife and children.

I note that the Appellant testified at the hearing that XXXX began to threaten him after his brother was killed on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2018. However, the Appellant did not leave Jamaica until XXXX months later, on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2018. There is no evidence in the record that the Appellant was ever approached by XXXX during this period of time or that any attempts were made to harm him while he was still in the Jamaica, despite being perceived to be an informer. The Appellant testified that he continued to work for XXXX weeks after his brother's death and remained living at the same residence until he left Jamaica. The Appellant wrote in his BOC that after his brother's death, people began making threats against his family, saying that they would kill them and burn down his house where he lived with his wife and children. However, there is no evidence in the record that he or his family were harmed in any way or that their house was set on fire. His family continue to reside in the same house and there is no evidence in the record that any attempts were made to harm any member of his family, beyond a threat made to his wife one year later on the street. The Appellant has provided no details, such as dates, places or number of occurrences, of any ongoing threats that were made to him or his family. The instructions for the BOC specifically asked the Appellant to provide these details.

Although the Appellant has alleged that it is his belief that he was being targeted because of a childhood friendship with a gang leader named XXXX, he has provided no corroboration of that friendship. Furthermore, the Appellant did not mention XXXX or XXXX in his BOC. I find it reasonable to expect that, if the Appellant was being targeted because of his relationship with a childhood friend, that information would be corroborated given that he made the effort to ask several family members to provide letters. I also find it reasonable to expect that if the Appellant was being targeted by a gang leader because of his childhood friendship with an opposing gang leader, this information would have been included in his BOC given that it goes to the heart of the allegations made at the hearing. Summary

I have considered that the Appellant's evidence regarding being targeted by a gang leader in Jamaica was vague and without detail. His testimony included no dates or specific incidents. He was unable to name the gang he feared, despite living in the neighbourhood the gang presided over all his life. He made no mention in his BOC that he was being targeted by a specific individual. I have also considered that despite his allegations in his BOC that both he and his family members were being targeted for death and that the house would be burnt down, there is no evidence that any attempts were made to harm the Appellant while he was in Jamaica for three months after his brother's death, or any member of his family since XXXX 2018. There is no evidence that the house where he resided was attacked in any way. His wife and children continue to reside in that house and it is reasonable to expect that if they believed that the house was going to be burnt down and they were going to be killed, they would leave that residence. Although the Appellant testified that a year after he left Jamaica, his wife was threatened on the street, there were few details both in the Appellant's testimony and in the letter from his wife that would support the Appellant's allegation that he is being targeted by a gang leader because he is thought to be an informer. The document from the police also does not support the Appellant's allegations, as it only notes the word "threat" and not the details of what happened and who was involved. The letters from the Appellant's mother and siblings provide no details of the Appellant being targeted by any specific individual or group.

I find, after considering the totality of the evidence in the record, that the Appellant has not established that he has a personalized risk of harm in Jamaica. He has not shown that a gang leader or gang members have a real intent to inflict serious harm upon him. I find that the risk upon return to Jamaica is a generalized one, based on the documentary evidence in the record regarding gang violence throughout the country and specifically in Kingston where the Appellant resided. As noted by the RPD, the country conditions documents12 in the record speak of an ongoing culture of violence in Jamaica, which is supported by the letters provided by the Appellant's family members. It is noted that Jamaicans face high levels of violence daily and that crime levels are particularly high around certain areas of Kingston and Montego Bay. It is noted that most violent crimes involve firearms and that Jamaica continued to grapple with persistent gang violence. It is stated that gang and vigilante violence remain a common occurrence in Jamaica.13 CONCLUSION

I have found, after conducting an independent assessment of the evidence, that the Appellant has not established a nexus to a Convention ground and that the risk of violence the Appellant faces upon return to Jamaica is a generalized one. I further find that there is not a serious possibility that he would be persecuted, should he return to Jamaica, nor would he be subjected personally, on a balance of probabilities, to a risk to life, a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment, or a danger of torture, should he return to Jamaica.

I dismiss the appeal and confirm the decision of the RPD that the Appellant is neither a Convention refugee, nor a person in need of protection, pursuant to paragraph 111(1)(a) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).
